assertion: A federal jury in San Diego found that Apple owes Taction Technology more than $5.7 billion for infringing two of its haptics patents (U.S. Patent Nos. 10,659,885 and 10,820,117).
warehouse_value: Patents US 10,659,885 and 10,820,117 exist, granted 2020-05-19 and 2020-10-27, titled 'Systems and methods for generating damped electromagnetically actuated planar motion for audio-frequency vibrations' -- consistent with the article's vibration/haptic transducer description
sql: SELECT patent_id, patent_date, patent_title FROM patents.patent_grants WHERE patent_id IN ('10659885','10820117')
independent_value: Exact verdict figure $5,721,961,750 (rounds to >$5.7B); case Taction Tech. Inc. v. Apple Inc., S.D. Cal. No. 3:21-cv-00812, verdict 9/25-9/26/26

sources.title: Bloomberg Law: Apple Owes $5.7 Billion for Infringement of Haptics Patents

assertion: Taction filed suit against Apple in 2021 in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of California; a judge dismissed the case in 2023, and the Federal Circuit revived it on appeal in 2025.
independent_value: AppleInsider dates the suit to April 2021; Bloomberg Law docket confirms S.D. Cal. No. 3:21-cv-00812; a San Diego federal judge dismissed the case (Aug. 2023 per Bloomberg Law); the Federal Circuit reversed that dismissal on Aug. 13, 2025 per Bloomberg Law's own prior story on the ruling

sources.title: Bloomberg Law: Apple's Win in Haptics Patent Case Undone by Federal Circuit

assertion: Apple's statement to CNBC read: 'While we thank the jury for their consideration, we strongly disagree with today's verdict and the damages awarded, which are entirely unsupported by the facts. Apple's Taptic Engine is fundamentally different from Taction's technology, which Taction's own testing of Apple's products confirmed during trial. Apple does not use Taction's technology, and we will appeal.'

assertion: Taction's lead counsel, Lance Yang, partner at Quinn Emanuel, told CNBC: 'We're happy the jury found for Taction and vindicated its patent rights. Taction waited five and a half years for this case to get to trial, so it was a long time coming.'

independent_value: AppleInsider independently quotes Lance Yang making the identical statement, and Quinn Emanuel's own attorney directory (fetched directly) confirms Yang is a real partner there. Separately, Bloomberg Law attributes a near-identical quote to a different Quinn Emanuel partner on the same case, Tigran Guledjian, and Taction's trial team included at least five named partners with no single one designated 'lead counsel' in any filing found. The quote itself and the speaker are verified; CNBC's 'lead counsel' label attributed to Yang is an unverified characterization -- this is the source of the fidelity issue in the split rating below (CNBC's framing of Yang's role/title), not an accuracy issue with what Yang actually said.
